title: Fame and fortune
translation: Some people let fame and money run their lives. They never get a moment's peace, and they wear themselves out until the day they die. That's foolish.

Money first. The more you own, the harder it is to keep yourself safe. Money buys you harm and brings trouble to your door. Leave a pile of gold high enough to prop up the stars, and after you're dead it will only be a headache for other people. The things that dazzle fools aren't worth much either. Big carriages, fat horses, gold and jewels: anyone with sense sees how stupid it all is. Throw the gold away in the mountains and drop the jewels in the river. Losing your head over money is the most foolish thing there is.

A name that lives on after you, now that seems worth having. But does a high rank make someone great? Fools and incompetents get born into the right family, get lucky, climb to the top and live in great style. And plenty of brilliant, truly wise people chose to stay at the bottom, or never got their chance, and that was the end of it. Wanting a high position above all else is foolish too, one step down.

What you'd really want to be remembered for is your wisdom and your character. But think about it. Loving fame just means you like hearing what people say about you. The people who praise you and the people who run you down won't be around for long, and the ones who hear it from them will soon be gone too. So who are you embarrassed in front of? Who is it you want to know your name? Besides, praise is where blame starts. A name that outlives you is no use at all. Wanting that is foolish too, one more step down.

Then there are the people who insist on wisdom and want to be clever. Here's what I'd say to them. Once cleverness shows up, lies come with it. Talent is just your cravings, grown bigger. What you hear from others and learn from books isn't real wisdom. So what is wisdom? Right and wrong are the same thing. And what is good? The truly wise person has no wisdom, no virtue, no achievements and no name. Who would know about him? Who would tell the story? It's not that he hides his virtue and plays the fool. He has simply never stood where clever and stupid, gain and loss, mean anything.
Go after fame and profit with a confused mind, and this is what you get. All of it is wrong. None of it is worth talking about, and none of it is worth wanting.

literal: Being used by fame and profit, with no quiet leisure, making one's whole life suffer: that is foolish.
If one's wealth is great, one is poor at protecting oneself.
It is a go-between that buys harm and invites trouble.
Even if after one's death one props up the Northern Dipper with gold, it will surely be a trouble for others.
Pleasures that delight the eyes of foolish people are also pointless.
Big carriages, fat horses, and ornaments of gold and jewels too: a person with a heart will surely see them as distastefully foolish.
Gold should be thrown away in the mountains, and jewels thrown into the deep water.
One who is led astray by profit is an exceedingly foolish person.
To leave a name that will not be buried for long ages: that would surely be desirable.
Should one call someone an excellent person just because his rank is high and noble?
Even foolish and inept people, if they are born into the (right) house and meet with the times, rise to high rank and reach the height of luxury.
Splendid wise men and sages who stayed in low rank by their own choice, or did not meet with their time and came to an end: these too are many.
To wish single-mindedly for high office and rank is next in foolishness.
One would like to leave an excellent reputation in the world for one's wisdom and heart, but if one thinks it over carefully, loving fame is delighting in what people say.
The people who praise and the people who slander will both not remain in the world, and the people who will hear of it in turn will also quickly depart.
Before whom should one feel shame, and by whom should one wish to be known?
Praise, moreover, is the source of slander.
A name remaining after one's death is of no use at all.
To wish for this is also next in foolishness.
But if I speak for people who stubbornly seek wisdom and wish for cleverness: when wisdom comes out, there is falsehood, and talent is the growth of worldly passions.
To hear by tradition and to know by study is not true wisdom.
What should be called wisdom?
Acceptable and unacceptable are one line.
What is called good?
The true person has no wisdom, no virtue, no merit and no name.
Who would know him, who would pass him on?
This is not hiding virtue and keeping to foolishness: it is because from the start he does not stand in the realm of wise and foolish, gain and loss.
When one seeks the essentials of fame and profit with a deluded mind, it is like this.
All things are wrong.
Not worth speaking of, not worth wishing for.

notes.text: {名利|みやうり}: 'fame and profit', a Buddhist word for the two things that keep people tied to the world. 'Being used by' them: the person is the servant, not the master. The section takes them apart one at a time: money, rank, fame, and finally cleverness.

notes.quote: 身の後には金をして北斗を支ふとも
notes.text: An allusion to a poem by the Chinese poet Bai Juyi (772–846): 'gold piled up after your death high enough to prop up the Northern Dipper is not worth one jar of wine while you live'. Kenkō uses the image but not the wine.

notes.quote: 金は山にすて、玉は淵になぐべし
notes.text: This echoes a line in the Chinese classic Zhuangzi about leaving gold in the mountains and pearls in the deep water. {淵|ふち}: a deep pool in a river.

{次|つぎ}に: 'next', the next step down. Money is the worst folly, wanting rank is one step down, and wanting fame (with the same phrase a little later) another step down. The translation keeps the ladder.

notes.quote: 勝れたる人とやはいふべき
notes.text: やは: a rhetorical question, 'should one call him…? (No.)'.

notes.quote: 身の後の名残りて更に益なし
notes.text: {更|さら}に … なし: 'not at all'. {益|やく}なし: 'useless'. The same word survives in modern {益|えき}, but the classical reading is usually やく.

notes.quote: 才能は煩悩の増長せるなり
notes.text: {煩悩|ぼんなう}: in Buddhism, the cravings and delusions that keep a person in the cycle of rebirth. Talent, in this view, is not a gift but more of the same problem.

'Acceptable and unacceptable are one line': the distinction itself is the mistake. This and the 'true person' who has no merit and no name come from the Zhuangzi, which says the perfect man has no self, the spirit man no merit, and the sage no name. Kenkō mixes Buddhist and Daoist ideas freely here.
{非|ひ}: 'wrong', and also 'not real'. Both meanings fit the ending. The last line has no verb of judgement at all, just two flat 'not worth it'.
